title: Pointers & Arrays: The Moving Cursor
description: Five ideas that turn a pointer into a cursor you can slide along an array.
congratsText: You can now aim a cursor at an array, slide it, write through it, and say exactly where a lone pointer falls short.
objectives: Explain what a pointer stores and how * differs from the pointer itself
Identify an array's name as the address of its first item
Predict how a write through a pointer changes the array behind it
Calculate where cursor + n lands in an array of ints
Contrast what sizeof, assignment, and bounds mean for an array versus a pointer
recap: A pointer holds an address; & gets one and * reads the value back
An array's name is already the address of its first item, so no & is needed to aim at it
*cursor and prices[1] are two labels on one box, so a write through either is seen by both
cursor + 1 jumps one whole int, which is what makes *(cursor + i) match prices[i]
sizeof sees a whole array but only one address of a pointer, and C never checks bounds for you

chunks.text: Every variable sits somewhere in memory, and that spot has a numeric address. The & operator hands you that address.
A pointer is a variable built to hold an address. int *cursor = &total; stores where total lives, not what it holds.

check.question: Is int *cursor = total; a valid way to aim a cursor?

chunks.text: *cursor means go to that address and look inside, so it gives a value. Plain cursor gives the location, printed with %p.

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: Nothing, cursor was never given a value

sections.title: The Array Name Is Already an Address

chunks.text: An array's name is the address of its first item, which is why prices and &prices[0] print the same address.
So a pointer is aimed at an array with no & at all. cursor = prices; is enough, because the name is already an address.

check.question: Do you need & when writing cursor = prices;?

chunks.text: Once aimed, *cursor and prices[0] are two labels on one box, so reading either gives the same number.
The star works on the left of = too. *cursor = 99; drops 99 into the box the cursor is parked on, and that box belongs to the array.
You never wrote prices[1] by name, yet it changed. A write through either label is seen by the other, because there is only one box.

check.question: Can prices[1] change without being named?

chunks.text: Drop the star and the meaning flips. cursor = 99; re-aims the cursor at address 99 instead of storing 99 anywhere.

check.question: cursor = 99; stores 99 in the box the cursor was on.

quiz.question: Arrange these lines so the last one prints 20.

chunks.text: cursor + 1 does not add one byte. It moves forward by one whole item, which is 4 bytes for an int.
That is why *(cursor + i) lands on the same item as prices[i]. The compiler rewrites brackets as pointer math anyway.

check.question: Brackets are shorthand for pointer math.

chunks.text: cursor++ makes the same jump but leaves the cursor there. Read, then slide, and a loop walks the whole shelf with no index at all.

check.question: After cursor++, the earlier match with prices[i] still lines up.

quiz.question: What does this print?

chunks.text: sizeof(prices) reports the whole shelf, 5 ints at 4 bytes each. sizeof(cursor) reports one address, usually 8 bytes.

check.question: sizeof on a pointer measures the whole array.

chunks.text: A pointer can be re-aimed any time, but an array name cannot be reassigned. prices = cursor; is refused outright.
C never checks bounds. Slide past slot 4 and the read still succeeds, printing whatever byte happened to be sitting there.

check.question: Who has to stop the walk in time?
